title: Fake News as Discursive Integration: An Analysis of Sites That Publish False, Misleading, Hyperpartisan and Sensational Information
screen_reason: Content analysis of 646 stories sampled from 46 US websites that had been labelled fake news (Zimdars list intersected with Newswhip's most-shared sites), covering two randomly constructed weeks of the 2016 election season plus 7-9 November 2016. Coders fact-checked each story's main claim on a five-point true-to-false scale, giving shares of items classified false: CONTENT. Because every story comes from a site already labelled fake news, the falsity shares are computed inside a misinformation-only sample, so all rows carry within_misinfo_content = true (R3, appendix only).

estimates.platform: Websites labelled fake news (46 sites), engagement measured on Facebook and Twitter
estimates.date: Two randomly constructed weeks of the 2016 election season plus 7-9 November 2016 (17 days)
estimates.measure_type: % of stories from fake news sites whose main body claim was coded completely false (verifiably untrue)
estimates.value_raw: 1.7% of the body's main claim being verifiably untrue
estimates.denominator: 646 stories sampled from 46 sites labelled fake news (proportionate systematic random sample of the 24,783 articles those sites published on the 17 sampled days, plus a 260-story top-up to reduce Breitbart's dominance)
estimates.definition: Coders summarised the article's main factual claim, checked it against reputable fact-checking sites and, failing that, mainstream media or official documents, and assigned the code 'False' (5) on a scale of True / Mostly true / Half true-Mixture / Mostly false / False
estimates.misinfo_def: "information presented as truthful initially but that turns out to be false later on" (Lewandowsky et al. 2013), with no requirement of intent to deceive
estimates.source_quote: Completely false stories were uncommon, with only 4.7% of head- lines being fake and 1.7% of the body’s main claim being verifiably untrue.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three teams of two trained undergraduate and graduate coders, each team coding different variables so categories could not contaminate each other; misinformation coded against PolitiFact/Snopes-style criteria after five training sessions; Krippendorff's alpha .83 (headline) and .82 (body), items averaged (Cronbach's alpha .93). Coders were told to err on the side of coding a claim true unless a counterclaim could be found, so the falsity shares are deliberately conservative.
estimates.moderator_quote: It is important to note that we opted to take a conservative approach for this variable; that is, only determine falsehoods when the counterclaim is available and erring on the side of believing a claim was true unless we could prove otherwise.
estimates.notes: The denominator is stories from sites already labelled fake news, so this is falsity within a misinformation-only sample (R3), not a population prevalence. The five falsity categories are mutually exclusive, not cumulative; the paper's own summary that 'about 50% of the stories contained some deviation from factual information' would be a cross-category sum, which R8 forbids, so it is not coded.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: the 'no misinformation at all' shares (53.8% of headlines, 56.5% of bodies) and the 'mostly true' (19.3% / 19.9%) and 'half true/mixture' (12.8% / 11.7%) categories - these are the true or partly-true side of the same distribution; combining them into a single misinformation share would be a cross-category sum, which R8 forbids. The authors' summary that 'about 50% of the stories contained some deviation from factual information' is such a sum, stated only approximately, so it was not coded either. Also not extracted: sensationalism (58% not sensational at all, about 6% moderate or high), clickbait (20.4% of stories), and the partisanship distribution (45.5% neutral, 30.7% slightly, 16.4% moderately, 7.5% extremely partisan) - none of these is a falsity judgement, and under the QUALITY rule they would not count as CONTENT. All engagement models (Tables 2 and 3) report associations, not shares. Judgement to flag: the whole sample is drawn from sites pre-labelled fake news, so every share here is a within-misinformation figure; the paper's headline finding is precisely that outright falsehood is rare inside that set.

rob.design: Population built by intersecting the Zimdars list of suspicious sites with Newswhip's 716 most-shared sites during 18 September to 7 November 2016 (22,000 stories), giving 117 sites, from which 50 were randomly selected. All stories from those sites for two randomly constructed weeks plus 7-9 November 2016 (24,783 articles over 17 days) formed the sampling frame; proportionate systematic random sampling gave N = 398, plus a purposive top-up of 260 stories from non-Breitbart sites, for a final 646 stories from 46 sites. Falsity, bias, sensationalism and clickbait coded by three separate two-person teams after five training sessions; reliability tested on 50 stories (Krippendorff's alpha .74-.91). Deliberately conservative falsity coding means some misinformation will have gone unflagged. Engagement metrics from Newswhip; mixed-effects models account for the nesting of stories within outlets. The authors flag that there is no agreed definition of fake news and that the Zimdars list has been criticised as skewed against conservative outlets.
rob.item6_quote: Coders were instructed to find factual error when possible. A scale (1 = True, 2 = Mostly true, 3 = Half true/Mixture, 4 = Mostly false, 5 = False, 99 = can’t determine) was adopted, based on the classification systems used by Politifact and Snopes, including consideration of dishonest reporting, i.e., stories with a grain of truth, but in which facts have been mischaracterized.
rob.item10_quote: Descriptive statistics reveal that 53.8% of headlines and 56.5% of body content did not contain misinformation at all.
